[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-REF-2.2.01.md#normative-language-convention]

### Normative Language Convention

This document and all Component ABBs in this hierarchy use normative language per [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119):

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **SHALL** | Mandatory — absolute obligation |
| **SHALL NOT** | Mandatory prohibition |
| **SHOULD** | Strongly recommended — deviation requires documented justification |
| **SHOULD NOT** | Strongly discouraged — deviation requires documented justification |
| **MAY** | Optional — permitted but not required |

> **Exception and Waiver Process**: Teams that cannot meet a SHALL requirement must submit a risk acceptance or waiver request through the established enterprise governance process. Waivers require documented risk justification and approval from appropriate security leadership or designated delegate. Temporary waivers must include a remediation timeline.

### ABB Context

- **This document**: Composite ABB — defines the full IAM architectural hierarchy
- **Domain**: Identity and Access Management — Security Domain
- **Capability Statement**: Establishes the architectural framework for managing digital identities, controlling access to enterprise resources, and enforcing continuous verification across all identity populations and environments in alignment with Zero Trust principles
page_texts.6:
[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-REF-2.2.01.md#abb-scope]

### ABB Scope

**In Scope**:

- Identity lifecycle management for workforce, partner, customer, and non-human identities
- Authentication architecture including MFA, phishing-resistant authenticators, and federated authentication
- Authorization architecture including RBAC, ABAC, and policy-based access decisions
- Relationship-aware authorization patterns for delegated, object-centric, and acting-on-behalf-of access flows
- Identity governance and administration including access reviews and entitlement management
- Credential and attribute management
- Identity federation and SSO across organizational boundaries
- Privileged access management and just-in-time access
- Identity proofing and assurance levels
- Non-human and AI system identity management
- Monitoring, logging, and analytics for identity-related events

**Out of Scope**:

- Vendor product selection and implementation-specific configuration (Phase E–F)
- Physical access control and facility security
- Network segmentation controls (see Network Security ABB)
- Data classification and data governance (see Information Security ABB)
- Security controls, configuration baselines, and compliance mandates (belong in `standards/security/`)
- Solution Building Blocks and product-specific tooling (Phase E–F outputs)

[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-REF-2.2.01.md#1-identity-is-the-control-plane]

#### 1. Identity is the Control Plane

All access decisions SHALL be rooted in a verified, continuously asserted identity. Network location, device ownership, or prior session state SHALL NOT constitute implicit trust. Every access request MUST be evaluated against the current identity context before a resource session is established, consistent with NIST SP 800-207.
page_texts.11:
[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-REF-2.2.01.md#2-least-privilege-across-all-identity-types]

#### 2. Least Privilege Across All Identity Types

Every identity—human, service account, AI agent, or device—SHALL be granted only the minimum permissions necessary to perform its defined function. Standing privilege SHALL NOT be the operational norm; just-in-time access with automatic revocation SHOULD be the architectural default. Role and attribute sets SHALL be reviewed on a defined cadence and revoked promptly upon role change or termination.
page_texts.12:
[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-REF-2.2.01.md#3-defense-in-depth-through-layered-identity-controls]

#### 3. Defense-in-Depth Through Layered Identity Controls

IAM controls SHALL be layered such that no single failure compromises the overall security posture. Authentication, authorization, lifecycle management, identity governance, and monitoring capabilities SHOULD operate as complementary, independently enforceable layers. The compromise of one layer SHALL not bypass the others.
page_texts.13:
[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-REF-2.2.01.md#4-identity-governance-as-a-continuous-process]

#### 4. Identity Governance as a Continuous Process

Access certifications, entitlement reviews, and policy enforcement SHALL be treated as continuous operational activities, not periodic events. Automated provisioning and deprovisioning workflows SHALL be the architectural default. Manual, unaudited access grants SHALL require documented justification and executive approval.

[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-REF-2.2.01.md#identity-lifecycle-management]

#### Identity Lifecycle Management

**Architectural intent**: Establish automated, authoritative workflows for creating, modifying, and deactivating identities for all principals across enterprise systems, ensuring that access rights reflect current organizational roles and relationships at all times.

**Design guidance**:

- Identity lifecycle workflows SHALL integrate with authoritative sources (HR systems, ERP, contract management) as the source of truth for identity attributes
- Provisioning and deprovisioning SHALL be automated; manual intervention SHOULD be the exception with an approval and audit trail
- Orphaned and stale accounts SHALL be detected and remediated through automated discovery and access review processes
- Role changes SHALL trigger access right recalculation; excess entitlements SHALL be revoked within a defined SLA
page_texts.16:
[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-REF-2.2.01.md#identity-governance-and-administration]

#### Identity Governance and Administration

**Architectural intent**: Provide centralized policy management, access review workflows, and entitlement intelligence that enforce least privilege and demonstrate compliance across the identity population.

**Design guidance**:

- Access certifications SHALL be conducted on a risk-proportionate schedule; privileged accounts SHOULD be reviewed at least quarterly
- Segregation of duties (SoD) policies SHALL be modeled, detected, and enforced at the entitlement level before access is granted
- Role definitions SHALL be business-aligned and auditable; unstructured, individual permission grants SHOULD be minimized
- Identity governance tooling SHALL produce evidence artifacts consumable by compliance and audit functions
page_texts.17:
[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-REF-2.2.01.md#authentication-services]

#### Authentication Services

**Architectural intent**: Verify the identity of every principal before any access is authorized, using authenticators appropriate to the assurance level required by the resource, and aligned with NIST SP 800-63B.

**Design guidance**:

- Single-factor authentication SHALL NOT be used for any system containing sensitive data or providing access to enterprise resources
- Authenticator strength SHALL be proportionate to the risk of the resource; privileged and high-sensitivity access SHALL require phishing-resistant authenticators (FIDO2/WebAuthn, PKI-based)
- Adaptive and risk-based authentication SHOULD be applied to detect anomalous access patterns and trigger step-up authentication dynamically
- Legacy authenticators (SMS OTP, voice OTP) SHALL have documented deprecation paths and SHOULD NOT be permitted for new implementations
page_texts.18:
[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-REF-2.2.01.md#authorization-services]

#### Authorization Services

**Architectural intent**: Enforce fine-grained, policy-driven access decisions for every resource request, using standardized models that support least privilege and dynamic context evaluation.

**Design guidance**:

- Authorization decisions SHALL be separated from authentication; an authenticated identity does not automatically imply authorization for any specific resource
- Role-based access control (RBAC) SHALL be the baseline authorization model; attribute-based access control (ABAC) SHOULD be applied where dynamic, context-sensitive access decisions are required; relationship-aware authorization constructs SHOULD be used for delegated and object-centric access scenarios
- Authorization policies SHALL be externalized from application code and centrally managed to ensure consistency and auditability
- Access decisions SHALL incorporate current context (device posture, location, time, risk signals) where technically feasible
page_texts.19:
[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-REF-2.2.01.md#credential-and-attribute-management]

#### Credential and Attribute Management

**Architectural intent**: Ensure that all credentials and identity attributes are issued, stored, rotated, and revoked through governed processes that protect their integrity and prevent unauthorized use.

**Design guidance**:

- Credentials SHALL be stored using cryptographic protections appropriate to their sensitivity; plaintext credential storage is prohibited
- Credential rotation SHALL be automated for non-human identities; human credentials SHOULD leverage passwordless or phishing-resistant mechanisms to reduce rotation burden
- Identity attributes SHALL be sourced from authoritative systems and synchronized through defined integration patterns; self-asserted attributes SHOULD NOT be used for access decisions without validation
- Certificate lifecycle (issuance, renewal, revocation) SHALL be managed through PKI infrastructure with defined procedures for emergency revocation
page_texts.20:
[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-REF-2.2.01.md#privileged-access-management]

#### Privileged Access Management

**Architectural intent**: Eliminate standing privilege for administrative and high-sensitivity access, replacing it with just-in-time, audited, and time-bounded access with comprehensive session visibility.

**Design guidance**:

- All privileged credentials SHALL be stored in a centralized vault with automated rotation
- Just-in-time access workflows SHALL be the architectural default for all administrative access to production systems
- Privileged sessions SHALL be brokered through a session management capability that provides recording, monitoring, and real-time termination capability
- Tiered administration boundaries SHALL be established to prevent privilege escalation across trust domains
page_texts.21:
[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-REF-2.2.01.md#identity-federation]

#### Identity Federation

**Architectural intent**: Enable secure, standards-based authentication across organizational boundaries by establishing governed trust relationships with external identity providers.

**Design guidance**:

- Federation SHALL be implemented using established standards (SAML 2.0, OpenID Connect, OAuth 2.0) per NIST SP 800-63C
- The enterprise SHALL maintain a centralized Identity Broker as the single federation gateway; applications SHALL NOT establish direct bilateral trust relationships with external IdPs without broker mediation
- Federation assertions SHALL be validated for signature, audience, issuance time, and replay protection at the broker; RPs SHALL NOT re-validate raw upstream assertions
- Federation Assurance Levels (FAL) SHALL be mapped to the sensitivity of the resources being accessed
page_texts.22:
[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-REF-2.2.01.md#single-sign-on]

#### Single Sign-On

**Architectural intent**: Reduce credential proliferation and authentication friction across applications by establishing a governed SSO architecture that maintains security posture throughout session lifecycles.

**Design guidance**:

- SSO SHALL be the architectural default for all applications requiring user authentication; non-federated local authentication is a security gap requiring remediation
- SSO sessions SHALL enforce idle timeout and absolute session limits proportionate to application sensitivity
- Single Logout (SLO) capability SHALL be implemented to enable centralized session termination across all active SP sessions
- Applications requiring elevated assurance for specific operations SHALL support step-up authentication without requiring full re-authentication
page_texts.23:
[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-REF-2.2.01.md#identity-monitoring-and-analytics]

#### Identity Monitoring and Analytics

**Architectural intent**: Provide continuous visibility into identity-related activities and access events, enabling timely detection of anomalous behavior, policy violations, and potential compromise.

**Design guidance**:

- All authentication attempts, authorization decisions, and administrative identity actions SHALL be logged to a centralized, tamper-resistant store
- Log retention periods SHALL satisfy regulatory requirements applicable to the systems and data accessed
- Identity analytics SHALL be integrated with enterprise SIEM capability to enable correlation, anomaly detection, and incident investigation
- Behavioral baselines SHALL be established for high-value identities (privileged users, service accounts, AI agents) to support anomaly detection

[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-REF-2.2.01.md#zero-trust-alignment-nist-sp-800-207]

### Zero Trust Alignment (NIST SP 800-207)

The IAM Composite ABB is the primary enabler of Zero Trust architecture across all five Zero Trust pillars:

- **Identity Pillar**: All five Component ABBs collectively establish the continuous verification model required by Zero Trust — identity must be verified before every access decision, regardless of network location
- **Devices Pillar**: Authentication and authorization decisions SHOULD incorporate device compliance signals from endpoint management platforms, conditioning access on verified device posture
- **Networks Pillar**: IAM controls are explicitly network-independent; trust is derived from verified identity and context, not network segment membership
- **Applications Pillar**: SSO and federation ABBs ensure that every application enforces the same authentication and authorization baseline regardless of hosting environment
- **Data Pillar**: Attribute-based authorization and identity proofing establish the verified identity foundation that data-centric access controls depend upon

page_texts.26:
[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-REF-2.2.01.md#nist-sp-800-53-intent-alignment]

### NIST SP 800-53 Intent Alignment

| Control Family | Architectural Intent |
|---|---|
| **AC — Access Control** | This ABB establishes the architectural capability for access enforcement, account lifecycle management, and least privilege that the AC family requires. Automated provisioning/deprovisioning directly enables AC-2; authorization architecture enables AC-3 and AC-6 |
| **IA — Identification and Authentication** | Authentication, MFA, identity proofing, and federation capabilities collectively address the full IA family intent — establishing unique identification, strong authentication, credential management, and identity assertion validation |
| **AU — Audit and Accountability** | Identity monitoring and analytics capability establishes the audit log generation, retention, and review architecture required by the AU family |
| **SC — System and Communications Protection** | Credential management, cryptographic binding (mTLS, DPoP), and PKI integration support the cryptographic protection intent of the SC family |
| **IR — Incident Response** | Session monitoring, anomaly detection, and automated revocation capabilities support the containment and recovery objectives of the IR family |
| **CM — Configuration Management** | Identity governance and entitlement management support the configuration-level access restriction intent expressed in CM-5 |

---
page_texts.27:
[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-REF-2.2.01.md#constraints-and-dependencies]

### Constraints and Dependencies

- **Identity Source Authority**: The IAM architecture depends on authoritative identity sources (HR, ERP, contract management). Gaps or delays in source system data will propagate into identity lifecycle accuracy; source system integration quality is a prerequisite for effective IAM
- **PKI and Cryptographic Infrastructure**: Credential management, certificate-based authentication, and federation assertion signing depend on a functioning enterprise PKI. PKI availability and certificate lifecycle management are foundational dependencies
- **Directory Services**: Authorization policy enforcement depends on current, accurate group membership and attribute data in directory services. Directory synchronization latency introduces windows of stale access
- **SIEM Integration**: Identity monitoring effectiveness is bounded by the quality of SIEM integration; IAM events must flow in near-real-time for anomaly detection to be operationally useful
- **Application Federation Readiness**: SSO and federation benefits can only be realized for applications that implement standards-based federation protocols; legacy applications with local authentication require migration investment
- **Cross-ABB Sequencing**: Identity Proofing (GUID-SEC-IAM-PROOFING-2.2.05) must be completed before credential issuance; MFA (GUID-SEC-IAM-MFA-2.2.04) must be configured before SSO session establishment for any application above IAL1
